title: Oracle to subscribe to Point Beach nuclear for the OpenAI Wisconsin campus
subtitle: The subscription deal — 10–20% of a 1960s-era Wisconsin reactor's output — routes nuclear power directly to a Stargate-tied AI data center, pending state approval.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: On October 2, Oracle and Wisconsin utility We Energies announced an agreement under which Oracle would subscribe to between 10% and 20% of the Point Beach Nuclear Plant's output — roughly 125 to 250 megawatts. The power is earmarked for the $15 billion Project Lighthouse campus in Port Washington, Wisconsin, which Oracle is co-developing with OpenAI and Vantage Data Centers as part of the Stargate build-out. Project Lighthouse is designed to house close to a gigawatt of AI capacity by 2028. The subscription still requires Wisconsin Public Service Commission approval.

Point Beach is Wisconsin's only active nuclear plant and dates to the late 1960s. Routing a double-digit percentage of its output to a single hyperscaler is a structural shift in how US baseload gets allocated — the plant was built to serve regional ratepayers, not a Stargate node. We Energies has already cited the Oracle agreement as a driver of its proposed 2027 rate case, including about 20% of a $176 million electric rate hike and roughly $59 million in fuel cost pass-through. Oracle counters that the subscription will save non-subscribing ratepayers approximately $300 million in fuel costs over the contract term.

This is one of several nuclear-to-AI deals in the past week — Meta signed up to 6.6 GW of nuclear capacity across three parallel deals — and the pattern is now visible: hyperscalers are no longer bidding against each other for marginal grid capacity, they are reserving named reactors. Expect state utility commissions, which traditionally see very little press coverage, to become critical AI policy venues. The question for Wisconsin regulators is whether a subscription contract to a single customer is categorically different from the industrial-rate class the plant has historically served.

A takeaway for learners: when you read 'a 1-gigawatt AI data center,' translate that to the energy supply decision behind it. One gigawatt is roughly the output of a mid-size nuclear reactor running flat out. The AI compute boom is now a direct consumer of generation capacity in the physical world, not an abstract cloud workload — and the permits, rate cases, and transmission upgrades that accompany it are now AI stories, not just utility stories.
